questions.question: When a river originates from a hill and flows in all directions, the drainage pattern is known as ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Radial.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Radial Pattern**__

 __
 
• The tributaries from a summit follow slope downwards and drain down in all directions.
 
• The radial drainage pattern develops around a central elevated point and is common to conically shaped features such as volcanoes.
 
• Examples: Streams of the Saurashtra region, the rivers originating from the Amarkantak Mountain, Central French Plateau, Mt. Kilimanjaro.
 
• The Narmada, Son and Mahanadi originate from Amarkantak Hills and flow in different directions.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Dendritic**__

 __
 
• This is an irregular tree branch shaped pattern that develops in a terrain that has uniform lithology and where faulting and jointing are insignificant.
 
• Examples: Indus, Godavari, Mahanadi, Cauvery, Krishna.
 
 
 
• **Trellis**__
 __
 
• In this type of pattern, the short subsequent streams meet the mainstream at right angles, and differential erosion through soft rocks paves the way for tributaries.
 
• Examples: The old folded mountains of the Singhbhum and Seine and its tributaries in the Paris basin have drainage of trellis pattern.
 
 
 
• **Centripetal**__
 
 
• In a low-lying basin, the streams converge from all sides.
 
• Examples: Streams of Ladakh, Tibet, and the Baghmati and its tributaries in Nepal.

questions.question: The area served by a canal system through supply of water for irrigation and other purposes is called a ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Command area.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Command Area**__

 __
 
• The area over which canal irrigation water flows by gravity is known as the command area.
 
• Types of Command areas in irrigation:
 
 
• **Gross Command Area**:
 
 
• It is the total area that can be economically irrigated from an irrigation scheme without considering the limitations of water.
 
• It is denoted by GCA.
 
• GCA= CCA + Uncultivable area 
 
 
 
• **Culturable Command Area**:
 
 
• A culturable area is an area in which a crop is grown at a particular time or crop season.
 
• It is denoted by CCA.
 
• CCA= GCA - Uncultivable area
 
 
 
• **Net Command Area**
 
 
• It is the Culturable Command Area obtained after the deduction of canal networks, supply ditches, etc constructed in the field.
 
• It is denoted by NCA.
 
• NCA= CCA - the area occupied by canals, networks, and ditches.
 
 
 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Irrigation**__

 
 
• Irrigation is supplying water artificially to the soil for the purpose of agricultural production.
 
• It is used in dry areas and during periods of inadequate rainfall.

questions.question: Identify the water harvesting system in Western Himalayas.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Guls**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Guls:-**

 
 
• **Guls are diversion channels that are built along the contours of hillsides to collect and transport water from streams and springs to villages and agricultural fields. **
 
• **The most common water harvesting system in the Western Himalayas is the gul, also known as a kul. **
 
• Guls are typically made of stone or earth and are lined with clay or plastic to prevent leakage.
 
• They can be several kilometers long and may have several branches to distribute water to different areas.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Johads:-**

 
 
• **These are traditional rainwater harvesting systems that are practiced in the states of Haryana, Rajasthan, Punjab, and western Uttar Pradesh of North India. **
 
• Johads are community-owned and managed, and they are used to store rainwater throughout the year.
 
 
 
• **Khadins:-**
 
 
• **These are traditional rainwater harvesting systems that are practiced in the Thar Desert region of India, particularly in the Jaisalmer district of Rajasthan.**
 
• Khadins are also known as dhoras.

questions.question: Which state ranks first with a total length of 31.2 thousand km of rivers and canals, which is about 17% of the total length of rivers and canals in the country?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Uttar Pradesh** ranks** first** in the country with a total length of** 31.2 thousand kilometers** of Rivers and Canals. This constitutes about **17%** of the total length of rivers and canals in India.
 
• The state is drained by two major rivers, the **Ganges and the Yamuna, **as well as a number of their significant tributaries such as the** Ghaghara, Gomti, Chambal, Betwa, and Ken.**
 
• Canals form an integral part of Uttar Pradesh's **irrigation system. **The Upper Ganges Canal, one of the oldest canals in India, and the Lower Ganges Canal are the lifeblood of swathes of agricultural land in the state.
 
• These rivers and canals play a critical role in supporting **agriculture**, which is the mainstay of the **state's economy, **providing necessary water for farming.
 
• The extensive network of rivers and canals also supports **fisheries and local commerce,** and holds cultural and religious significance, with towns like **Varanasi and Allahabad** being significant religious hubs due to their location on the banks of the** Ganga and Yamuna rivers **respectively.
 
• However, water management remains a significant challenge, with issues of drought in some areas and floods in others due to variable rainfall and limited storage capacity.

questions.question: Tila, Seti and Beri are the tributaries of:

__
 
• **Ghaghara River:**

 
 
• The Ghaghara, known as **Karnali in Nepal**, is a major left-bank tributary of the Ganga.
 
• It originates near **Mansarovar Lake in Tibet** and flows through Nepal before entering India.
 
• In India, it flows through **Uttar Pradesh and Bihar** and finally joins the Ganga at **Chhapra**.
 
• **Tila, Seti, and Beri** are its important tributaries in Nepal, making Ghaghara the correct answer.

• Also known as the **Tons River**, it is a tributary of the Ganga.
 
• It originates from the **Tamsa Kund** in the **Kaimur range** of Madhya Pradesh.
 
• After a hilly journey of about **64 km**, it enters the plains and is joined by the **Belan River**.
 
• It merges with the **Ganga near Sirsa**, about 32 km from Prayagraj (U.P.).
 
• The Tamsa is historically significant, as traditions associate it with Lord Rama’s exile journey.
 
• However, it does not have tributaries like Tila, Seti, and Beri, so it is not the correct answer.
 
 
 
• **Mahi River:**
 
 
• Originates in Madhya Pradesh, flows through Rajasthan and Gujarat, and drains into the Arabian Sea.
 
• Its tributaries include Som and Anas, not Tila, Seti, or Beri.
 
 
 
• **Sabarmati River:**
 
 
• Originates from the Aravalli Hills in Rajasthan and flows into Gujarat before meeting the Arabian Sea.
 
• Its tributaries include Hathmati, Wakal, and Sei, not Tila, Seti, or Beri.

questions.question: Aner, Panzara and Waghur are the tributaries of which river?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Tapi**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** Tapi 

__
 
• Tapi is a central Indian river.
 
• It is one of the most important rivers of peninsular India with the run from east to west.
 
• It originates in the Eastern Satpura Range of southern Madhya Pradesh state.
 
• It flows in a westward direction, draining some important historic places like Madhya Pradesh’s Nimar region, East Vidarbha region, and Maharashtra’s Khandesh in the northwest corner of the Deccan Plateau and South Gujarat before draining into the Gulf of Cambay of the Arabian Sea.
 
• The River Basin of Tapi River lies mostly in the eastern and northern districts of Maharashtra state.
 
• The river also covers some districts of Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat as well.
 
• The principal tributaries of Tapi River are Waghur River, Aner River, Girna River, Purna River, Panzara River and Bori River.​

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• Mahanadi

 
 
• Mahanadi River is a river in central India, rising in the hills of southeastern Chhattisgarh state.
 
• The Origin of Mahanadi is from Raipur, Chhattisgarh.
 
• It has a total course of 858 kilometers (533 mi).
 
• The river originates from Sihawa Mountain in Chhattisgarh. 
 
• The river flows through the states of Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, and Odisha.
 
• The largest dam, the Hirakud Dam is built on the river.
 
• The principal tributaries of the Mahanadi River are; Sheonath, Jonk, Hasdeo, Mand, Ib, Ong, Tel.
 
• The Mahanadi basin extends over an area of 141,589 km2 which is nearly 4.3% of the total geographical area of the country.
 
• The Mahanadi river ranks second to the Godavari river among the peninsular rivers in respect of water potential.
 
• It lies between east longitudes 80° 30' to 86° 50' and north latitudes 19° 21' to 23° 35'.
 
 
 
• Godavari​​
 
 
• The Godavari is India's second-longest river, approximately 1,465 kilometers long, after the Ganges River.
 
• It originates from Trimbakeshwar, Nashik in Maharashtra.
 
• The river flows in the eastern direction through the states of Maharashtra, Telangana, and Andhra Pradesh, and empties into the Bay of Bengal.
 
• It is also known as 'Dakshina Ganga' and 'Vriddha Ganga' due to its large size and extent.
 
• The Godavari River basin is the third-largest in India, covering about 10% of India's total geographical area.
 
• The river has a total of twelve sub-basins, divided by the Krishna - Godavari Commission.
 
• Key tributaries of the Godavari include the Trimbakeshwar, Purna, Pravara, Indravati, Sabari, Penganga, Maner, and Wardha.

__

• The ancient Mahadev temple in Mahabaleshwar is dedicated to Lord Shiva, one of the principal deities in Hinduism.

• Mahabaleshwar, located in the Satara district of Maharashtra, is a popular hill station and pilgrimage site.
 
 
 
• **Krishna River**
 
 
• The Krishna River is one of the longest rivers in India, with a total length of about 1,400 kilometers (870 miles).

• The river basin is a critical water source for irrigation, drinking water, and hydroelectric power generation.

• **Significance of River Basins**
 
 
• A river basin is the land area drained by a river and its tributaries, playing a crucial role in the hydrological cycle.

• Management and conservation of river basins are essential for sustainable water resources and environmental health.

questions.question: Which of the following are west flowing rivers?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Mahi and Sabarmati**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Mahi River is one of the major west-flowing rivers in India, flowing through the states of Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, and Gujarat before draining into the Arabian Sea.
 
• The Sabarmati River originates in the Aravalli Range of the Udaipur District of Rajasthan and flows into the Gulf of Khambhat in the Arabian Sea, making it a west-flowing river.
 
• Both rivers play a crucial role in the irrigation and water supply for the regions they flow through, supporting agriculture and local communities.
 
• West-flowing rivers like Mahi and Sabarmati are less common in India compared to the east-flowing rivers, which generally drain into the Bay of Bengal.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **West Flowing Rivers in India**

 
 
• Most of the rivers in India flow eastwards towards the Bay of Bengal. However, there are a few significant rivers that flow westwards and drain into the Arabian Sea.
 
• Besides Mahi and Sabarmati, other notable west-flowing rivers include the Narmada and the Tapti.
 
• The Narmada River is one of the largest west-flowing rivers in India, originating from the Amarkantak Plateau and flowing through Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat before emptying into the Arabian Sea.
 
• The Tapti River originates from the Satpura Range of Madhya Pradesh and flows westward through Maharashtra and Gujarat, also draining into the Arabian Sea.
 
 
 
• **Importance of River Systems**
 
 
• Rivers are vital for the ecosystem as they provide water for drinking, irrigation, and industrial purposes.
 
• They also support a diverse range of flora and fauna, contributing to biodiversity.
 
• Rivers play a crucial role in shaping the landscape, influencing soil fertility and agricultural productivity.
 
• Many civilizations have historically settled along riverbanks, benefiting from the natural resources and transportation routes provided by rivers.
 
 
 
• **Challenges Facing River Systems**
 
 
• Pollution from industrial, agricultural, and domestic sources poses a significant threat to river ecosystems.
 
• Over-extraction of water for irrigation and other uses can lead to reduced water flow, affecting both human and ecological health.
 
• Climate change impacts, such as altered precipitation patterns and increased frequency of extreme weather events, can affect river flow and water availability.
 
• Efforts to manage and conserve river systems involve integrated water resource management, pollution control measures, and conservation initiatives to protect and restore river ecosystems.

questions.question: The drainage system formed when rivers discharge their waters from all directions in a lake or depression, as in the case of Loktak Lake in Manipur, is called ________.
questions.solution:
The Correct Answer is **centripetal.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__****Centripetal Drainage Pattern:**

__
 
• It is just the opposite of the radial as streams flow toward a central depression.
 
• During wetter portions of the year, these streams feed ephemeral lakes, which evaporate away during dry periods.
 
• Sometimes, salt flats are also created in these dry lake beds as salt dissolved in the lake water precipitates out of solution and is left behind when the water evaporates away.
 
• **E.g. Loktak lake in Manipur.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

**Radial Drainage Pattern:**

 
• The radial drainage pattern develops around a central elevated point and is common to conically shaped features such as volcanoes.
 
• When the rivers originate from a hill and flow in all directions, the drainage pattern is known as ‘radial’.
 
• E.g. The rivers originating from the** Amarkantak range; Narmada** and **Son (tributary of Ganga).**

**Trellis Drainage Pattern:**

 
• Trellis drainage develops in folded topography where hard and soft rocks exist parallel to each other.
 
• Down-turned folds called synclines form valleys in which reside the main channel of the stream.
 
• Such a pattern is formed when the primary tributaries of main rivers flow parallel to each other and secondary tributaries join them at right angles.
 
• **E.g. The rivers in the upper part of the Himalayan region; Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra.**

**Dendritic Drainage Pattern:**

 
• It is the most common form and resembles the branching pattern of tree roots.
 
• The dendritic pattern develops where the river channel follows the slope of the terrain.
 
• The pattern develops in areas where the rock beneath the stream has no particular structure and can be eroded equally easily in all directions.
 
• Tributaries join larger streams at acute angles (less than 90°).
 
• **E.g. The rivers of the northern plains; Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra.**
